title: Writing Systems of the World
intro: Ten questions on the scripts the world writes in, from Devanagari to Thaana. The most common script of each language is the one named in the answer. Every answer shows its source.

questions.prompt: Which script is most commonly used to write Hindi?
questions.explain: Hindi is most commonly written in the Devanagari script, which Nepali and Marathi also use.

questions.prompt: Which script is most commonly used to write Russian?
questions.explain: Russian is written in the Cyrillic script, as are Bulgarian and Ukrainian.

questions.prompt: Which script is most commonly used to write Greek?
questions.explain: Greek is written in its own script, also called Greek, rather than in Cyrillic, Georgian or Hebrew.

questions.prompt: Which script is most commonly used to write Amharic, an official language of Ethiopia?
questions.explain: Amharic is written in the Ethiopic script, also used for Tigrinya.

questions.prompt: Georgian is written in its own script. What is that script called?
questions.explain: Georgian has its own script, called Georgian; Armenian is likewise written in the Armenian script.

questions.prompt: Which script is most commonly used to write Dzongkha, an official language of Bhutan?
questions.explain: Dzongkha is written in the Tibetan script, as is the Tibetan language itself.

questions.prompt: Which script is most commonly used to write Dhivehi, an official language of the Maldives?
questions.explain: Dhivehi is most commonly written in the Thaana script, not in Arabic, Sinhala or Devanagari.

questions.prompt: Which of these scripts is used to write Tamil?
questions.explain: Tamil has its own script; Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam each have theirs too.

questions.prompt: Which script is most commonly used to write Khmer, an official language of Cambodia?
questions.explain: Khmer has its own script, called Khmer; Thai, Lao and Burmese have different ones.

questions.prompt: Which of these languages is written in the Armenian script?
questions.explain: Armenian has its own script; Georgian, Hebrew and Greek each use another.
